{{Short description|Polynomial with reversed root positions}}
{{More citations needed|date=April 2021}}
In [[algebra]], given a [[polynomial]]
<math display=block>p(x) = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \cdots + a_nx^n,</math>
with [[coefficient]]s from an arbitrary [[Field (mathematics)|field]], its '''reciprocal polynomial''' or '''reflected polynomial''',<ref name="concrete">*{{cite book | last1 = Graham | first1 = Ronald |author-link=Ronald Graham |last2=Knuth|first2=Donald E.|author-link2=Donald Knuth|last3=Patashnik|first3=Oren | title = Concrete mathematics : a foundation for computer science | edition=Second | publisher = Addison-Wesley | location = Reading, Mass | year = 1994 | isbn = 978-0201558029 | page= 340}}</ref><ref name="Aigner">{{cite book | last = Aigner | first = Martin | title = A course in enumeration | publisher = Springer | location = Berlin New York | year = 2007 | isbn = 978-3540390329 | page = 94 }}</ref> denoted by {{math|''p''<sup>∗</sup>}} or {{math|''p''<sup>R</sup>}},<ref name="Aigner"/><ref name="concrete"/> is the polynomial with the same coefficients in the reverse order,<ref>{{harvnb|Roman|1995|loc=pg.37}}</ref>

<math display=block>p^*(x) = a_n + a_{n-1}x + \cdots + a_0x^n = x^n p(x^{-1}).</math>

That is, the coefficients of <math>p^*</math> are the coefficients of <math>p</math> in reverse order. Reciprocal polynomials arise naturally in [[linear algebra]] as the [[characteristic polynomial]] of the [[inverse of a matrix]].

In the special case where the field is the [[complex number]]s, when

<math display=block>p(z) = a_0 + a_1z + a_2z^2 + \cdots + a_nz^n,</math>

the '''conjugate reciprocal polynomial''', denoted <math>p^\dagger</math>, is defined by,

<math display=block>p^{\dagger}(z) = \overline{a_n} + \overline{a_{n-1}}z + \cdots + \overline{a_0}z^n = z^n\overline{p(\bar{z}^{-1})},</math>

where <math>\overline{a_i}</math> denotes the [[complex conjugate]] of <math>a_i</math>, and is also called the reciprocal polynomial when no confusion can arise.

A polynomial <math>p</math> is called '''self-reciprocal''' or '''palindromic''' if <math>p(x)=p^*(x)</math>.
The coefficients of a self-reciprocal polynomial satisfy <math>a_i=a_{n-i}</math> for all {{math|''i''}}.

== Properties ==
Reciprocal polynomials have several connections with their original polynomials, including:
# <math>\deg p=\deg p^*</math> if <math>a_0</math> is not 0.
# <math>p(x)=x^np^*(x^{-1})</math>.<ref name="Aigner"/>
# <math>\alpha</math> is a [[zero of a function|root]] of a polynomial <math>p</math> if and only if <math>\alpha^{-1}</math> is a root of <math>p^*</math> or if <math>\alpha=0</math> and <math>p^*</math> is of lower degree than <math>p</math>.<ref name="Pless 1990 loc=pg. 57">{{harvnb|Pless|1990|loc=pg. 57}}</ref>
# If <math>x\nmid p(x)</math> then <math>p</math> is [[Irreducible polynomial|irreducible]] if and only if <math>p^*</math> is irreducible.<ref name="Roman 1995 loc= pg. 37">{{harvnb|Roman|1995|loc= pg. 37}}</ref>
# <math>p</math> is [[Primitive polynomial (field theory)|primitive]] if and only if <math>p^*</math> is primitive.<ref name="Pless 1990 loc=pg. 57"/>

Other properties of reciprocal polynomials may be obtained, for instance:
* A self-reciprocal polynomial of odd degree is divisible by <math>x+1</math>, hence is not irreducible if its degree is <math>>1</math>.

==<span class="anchor" id="Palindromic polynomial"></span><span class="anchor" id="Antipalindromic polynomial"></span> Palindromic and antipalindromic polynomials==
A self-reciprocal polynomial is also called palindromic because its coefficients, when the polynomial is written in the order of ascending or descending powers, form a [[palindrome]]. That is, if
<math display=block> P(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^i</math> 
is a polynomial of [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] <math>n</math>, then <math>P</math> is ''palindromic'' if <math>a_i=a_{n-i}</math> for <math>i=0,1,\dots,n</math>, or equivalently if <math>P(x)=P^*(x)</math>. 

Similarly, a polynomial <math>P</math> of degree <math>n</math> is called '''antipalindromic''' if <math>a_i=-a_{n-i}</math> for <math>i=0,1,\dots,n</math>. That is, a polynomial <math>P</math> is ''antipalindromic'' if <math>P(x)=-P^*(x)</math>.

===Examples===
From the properties of the [[binomial coefficient]]s, it follows that the polynomials <math>P(x)=(x+1)^n</math> are palindromic for all positive [[integer]]s <math>n</math>, while the polynomials <math>Q(x)=(x-1)^n</math> are palindromic when <math>n</math> is even and antipalindromic when <math>n</math> is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]].

Other examples of palindromic polynomials include [[cyclotomic polynomial]]s and [[Eulerian polynomial]]s.

===Properties===
* If <math>a</math> is a root of a polynomial that is either palindromic or antipalindromic, then <math>\tfrac1a</math> is also a root and has the same [[multiplicity (mathematics)|multiplicity]].<ref>{{harvnb|Pless|1990|loc=pg. 57}} for the palindromic case only</ref>
* The converse is true: If for each root <math>a</math> of polynomial, the value <math>\tfrac1a</math> is also a root of the same multiplicity, then the polynomial is either palindromic or antipalindromic.
* For any polynomial <math>q</math>, the polynomial <math>q+q^*</math> is palindromic and the polynomial <math>q-q^*</math> is antipalindromic.
* It follows that any polynomial <math>q</math> can be written as the sum of a palindromic and an antipalindromic polynomial, since<ref>{{citation|first=Jonathan Y.|last=Stein|title=Digital Signal Processing: A Computer Science Perspective|publisher=Wiley Interscience|year=2000|page=384|isbn=9780471295464}}</ref>
<math display=block>q=\frac{q+q^*}{2}+\frac{q-q^*}{2}.</math>
* The product of two palindromic or antipalindromic polynomials is palindromic.
* The product of a palindromic polynomial and an antipalindromic polynomial is antipalindromic.
* A palindromic polynomial of odd degree is a multiple of <math>x+1</math> (it has <math>-1</math> as a root) and its quotient by <math>x+1</math> is also palindromic.
* An antipalindromic polynomial over a field <math>k</math> with odd [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] is a multiple of <math>x-1</math> (it has <math>1</math> as a root) and its quotient by <math>x-1</math> is palindromic.
* An antipalindromic polynomial of even degree is a multiple of <math>x^2-1</math> (it has <math>-1</math> and <math>1</math> as roots) and its quotient by <math>x^2-1</math> is palindromic. 
* If <math>p(x)</math> is a palindromic polynomial of even degree <math>2d</math>, then there is a polynomial <math>q</math> of degree <math>d</math> such that <math>p(x)=x^dq(x+\tfrac1x)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Durand|1961}}</ref>
* If <math>p(x)</math> is a [[monic polynomial|monic]] antipalindromic polynomial of even degree <math>2d</math> over a field <math>k</math> of odd [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]], then it can be written uniquely as <math>p(x)=x^d\bigl(Q(x)-Q(\tfrac1x)\bigr)</math>, where <math>Q</math> is a monic polynomial of degree <math>d</math> with no constant term.<ref>{{citation|first=Nicholas M.|last=Katz|author-link=Nick Katz|title=Convolution and Equidistribution : Sato-Tate Theorems for Finite Field Mellin Transformations|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2012|isbn=9780691153315|page=146}}</ref>
* If an antipalindromic polynomial <math>P</math> has even degree <math>2n</math> over a field <math>k</math> of odd characteristic, then its "middle" coefficient (of power <math>n</math> is <math>0</math> since <math>a_n=-a_{2n-n}</math>.

===Real coefficients===
A polynomial with [[Real number|real]] coefficients all of whose [[Complex number|complex]] roots lie on the unit circle in the [[complex plane]] (that is, all the roots have modulus 1) is either palindromic or antipalindromic.<ref>{{cite book|first1=Ivan|last1=Markovsky|first2=Shodhan|last2=Rao|title=2008 16th Mediterranean Conference on Control and Automation |chapter=Palindromic polynomials, time-reversible systems, and conserved quantities |publisher=IEEE|pages=125–130|year=2008|doi=10.1109/MED.2008.4602018|isbn=978-1-4244-2504-4|s2cid=14122451 |url=https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/266592/1/Med08.pdf}}</ref>

==Conjugate reciprocal polynomials{{anchor|Conjugate}}==

A polynomial is '''conjugate reciprocal''' if <math>p(x) \equiv p^{\dagger}(x)</math> and '''self-inversive''' if <math>p(x) = \omega p^{\dagger}(x)</math> for a scale factor <math>\omega</math> on the [[unit circle]].<ref name=SV08>{{cite book | last1=Sinclair | first1=Christopher D. | last2=Vaaler | first2=Jeffrey D. | chapter=Self-inversive polynomials with all zeros on the unit circle | zbl=1334.11017 | editor1-last=McKee | editor1-first=James | editor2-last=Smyth | editor2-first=C. J. | title=Number theory and polynomials. Proceedings of the workshop, Bristol, UK, April 3–7, 2006 | location=Cambridge | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn=978-0-521-71467-9 | series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series | volume=352 | pages=312–321 | year=2008 }}</ref>

If <math>p(z)</math> is the [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] of <math>z_0</math> with <math>|z_0|=1</math>, <math>z_0\ne 1</math>, and <math>p(z)</math> has [[real number|real]] coefficients, then <math>p(z)</math> is conjugate-reciprocal.  This follows because

<math display=block>z_0^n\overline{p(1/\bar{z_0})} = z_0^n\overline{p(z_0)} = z_0^n\bar{0} = 0.</math>

So <math>z_0</math> is a root of the polynomial <math>z^n\overline{p(\bar{z}^{-1})}</math> which has degree <math>n</math>.  But, the minimal polynomial is unique, hence 
<math display=block>cp(z) = z^n\overline{p(\bar{z}^{-1})}</math>
for some constant <math>c</math>, i.e. <math>ca_i=\overline{a_{n-i}}=a_{n-i}</math>. Sum from <math>i=0</math> to <math>n</math> and note that <math>1</math> is not a root of <math>p</math>. We conclude that <math>c=1</math>.

A consequence is that the [[cyclotomic polynomial]]s <math>\Phi_n</math> are conjugate-reciprocal for <math>n>1</math>. This is used in the [[special number field sieve]] to allow numbers of the form <math>x^{11}\pm 1</math>, <math>x^{13}\pm 1</math>, <math>x^{15}\pm 1</math> and <math>x^{21}\pm 1</math> to be factored taking advantage of the algebraic factors by using polynomials of degree 5, 6, 4 and 6 respectively – note that <math>\varphi</math> ([[Euler's totient function]]) of the exponents are 10, 12, 8 and 12.{{Citation needed|date=November 2021}}

Per [[Cohn's theorem]], a self-inversive polynomial has as many roots in the [[unit disk]] <math>\{z\in\mathbb{C}: |z| < 1\}</math> as the reciprocal polynomial of its [[derivative]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ancochea|first=Germán|date=1953|title=Zeros of self-inversive polynomials|url=https://www.ams.org/proc/1953-004-06/S0002-9939-1953-0058748-8/|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=4|issue=6|pages=900–902|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1953-0058748-8|issn=0002-9939|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bonsall|first1=F. F.|last2=Marden|first2=Morris|date=1952|title=Zeros of self-inversive polynomials|url=https://www.ams.org/proc/1952-003-03/S0002-9939-1952-0047828-8/|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=3|issue=3|pages=471–475|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1952-0047828-8|issn=0002-9939|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Application in coding theory==

The reciprocal polynomial finds a use in the theory of [[Cyclic code|cyclic error correcting codes]]. Suppose <math>x^n-1</math> can be factored into the product of two polynomials, say <math>x^n-1=g(x)p(x)</math>. When <math>g(x)</math> generates a cyclic code <math>C</math>, then the reciprocal polynomial <math>p^*</math> generates <math>C^\perp</math>, the [[orthogonal complement]] of <math>C</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Pless|1990|loc = pg. 75, Theorem 48}}</ref>
Also, <math>C</math> is ''self-orthogonal'' (that is, <math>C\subseteq C^\perp</math>), if and only if  <math>p^*</math> divides <math>g(x)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Pless|1990|loc = pg. 77, Theorem 51}}</ref>
